National Weather Service Peachtree City GA
152 PM EDT Sat Oct 17 2026


...Afternoon Area Forecast Discussion...

.KEY MESSAGES...
 
  - Breezy winds will linger into the evening.

  - A Frost Advisory is in effect for the mountains of northeast
    Georgia. Near-freezing temperatures and the first frost of the
    season are likely along ridgelines, in valleys, and other 
    sheltered areas.

  - Mostly clear and dry conditions will persist for the next 7
    days.

&&

.SHORT TERM...
(This afternoon through Sunday)
Issued at 149 PM EDT Sat Oct 17 2026

North and central Georgia are solidly post-frontal, with supremely 
dry air (PWAT of 0.32" measured on this morning's 12Z sounding, well 
below the 10th percentile climatologically) overspreading the 
Southeast in its wake. Encroaching mid-level ridging and surface 
high pressure will support mostly clear, dry, and increasingly 
less breezy conditions for the remainder of the weekend. Highs 
today and tomorrow will be pleasant, in the upper 50s to near 70. 
As the core of the cold/dry airmass moves in overnight -- 
coincident with prime conditions for radiational cooling under 
clear skies -- our chilliest morning of the season is to come on 
Sunday: with lows in the mid-30s to 40s. A Frost Advisory has been
issued for portions of northeast Georgia where slackening winds 
(especially in sheltered areas) and temperatures at or below 36 
will support at least patchy frost formation tonight. 

Care has been taken to account for strong mixing post-front (that 
often overperforms available model guidance), and dewpoints are 
likely to plunge into the upper-20s to 30s for some on Sunday. 
Portions of the area may approach critical thresholds for fire 
weather tomorrow afternoon, and product issuance may be necessitated 
-- especially if gusts linger through Sunday. 

&&

.LONG TERM...
(Monday morning through next Friday)
Issued at 149 PM EDT Sat Oct 17 2026

Dry and Gradually Warming Next Week:

Guidance remains in good agreement on the forecast for much of next 
week, with a closed mid-level low within broader troughing over the 
East Coast. North and Central GA will remain dry in this setup, as 
north-northeast flow keeps PWATs below 0.5" and rain chances near 
zero. Temperatures will slowly warm each day, but remain right 
around normal, with highs slowly climbing from the mid to upper 60s 
on Monday, to the mid to upper 70s by mid to late week. Overnight 
lows will remain fairly crisp, ranging from the low to mid 40s early 
in the week, to the upper 40s by late week.

&&

out of nearly due N thru the aftn, weakly favoring the NE side 
for northern terminals. Exp 15G25KT to prevail thru 00Z, 
slackening slightly to 9-12KT with gusts tapering off overnight.

- 2) A Nor'easter lurks nearby for the new workweek bringing the

.DISCUSSION...
KEY MESSAGE 1...Below normal temperatures with frost and freeze
concerns continue through Monday morning.

The mid level trough axis is moving across the area this 
afternoon. Anafrontal rain is now exiting southern Maryland. 
Drier air in the wake of the upper jet streak is seen in water 
vapor imagery, with the clearing line reaching the I-95 
corridor. Temperatures are holding in the 50s this afternoon, 
although more sunshine and deep mixing have allowed them to warm
a few degrees higher than the previous forecast. Northerly 
winds gusting 20-35 mph continue through the afternoon before 
decreasing tonight.

The trends has continued tonight to keep the center of the
surface high over the upper Ohio Valley. There will be a sharper
pressure gradient on its southeastern flank due to the
developing Nor'easter off the North Carolina coast. While it was
already expected to some extent, winds remaining at least 5 mph
will likely limit how much temperatures can fall east of the 
Blue Ridge. Tonight's cold air will be driven more by advection,
although more widespread decoupling may occur west of the Blue 
Ridge closer to the surface high. The elevated winds may 
maintain notable temperature/dew point spreads (the latter of 
which will be in the upper 20s) to prevent widespread frost 
formation, especially east of the Blue Ridge. The Frost Advisory
remains in effect though, since many of these areas in the 
piedmont are prone to localized decoupling. While NBM 
probabilities of freezing temperatures have decreased from 
yesterday, especially east of the Blue Ridge, reliable guidance 
does still show pockets of freezing temperatures in the Freeze 
Warning area. The highest confidence in widespread subfreezing 
temperatures is in the Allegheny and Potomac Highlands, perhaps 
over to the central Shenandoah Valley. So in the end, no changes
to those headlines at this time.

The high settles more directly over the area Sunday into Sunday
night, leading to lighter winds and continued dry conditions.
The pressure gradient will increase to the southeast though, so
winds may be a bit more elevated over southern Maryland. Highs
will remain below normal in the mid 50s to near 60. The 
position of the high might actually lead to colder conditions in
some areas Sunday night into Monday morning, especially between
I-81 and US-15. Dew points in the upper 20s and lower 30s along
with calm winds make a case for more potential for frost and 
freeze conditions west of I-95. Headline decisions will need to
wait until it is determined where the growing season will
continue after tonight.

A gradual warming trend likely starts thereafter, although
temperatures will remain below normal through Monday night. 
While there is some uncertainty with the Nor'easter off the 
Carolina coast, most guidance keeps it far enough to the 
southeast for dry conditions to continue through Monday night.

KEY MESSAGE 2...A Nor'easter lurks nearby for the new workweek
bringing the potential for a few showers and breezy conditions,
especially along and east of I-95.

Uncertainty remains regarding a potential nor'easter developing in 
the vicinity of the NC/VA coast during the early and middle part of 
next week. The track of this system will dictate any rain chances, 
breezy conditions, and coastal flooding risks across the region. 
Current 12z guidance remains all over the place when it comes to the 
placement of the low and timing as it meanders along the coast. Each 
of the models form a coastal low on what was the residual upper 
level trough and front from earlier in the weekend. Guidance points 
to a low either along the coast of NC or 25-50 miles offshore Monday 
before drifting it north toward the Delmarva and NJ coast midweek. 
Some of the guidance even retrogrades the low back into southern NJ 
and the Delmarva during the back half of the workweek period. 
Meanwhile, 1035-1037 mb high pressure will remain wedged along 
and west of the mountains Monday into Tuesday before retreating 
east midweek. A secondary area of 1028-1030 mb Canadian high 
pressure will follow Wednesday and Thursday as it slides east 
from Ontario into New England before wedging south late week. 
It's not until next week when a front crosses the region. 

Synoptically, we sit in an omega block type setup under 
predominantly zonal flow. The coastal low offshore combined with the 
wedging high in the east, ridging in the center part of the country, 
and troughiness in the west. With that said, expect the nor'easter 
to have little movement along the coast throughout the week. As the 
low fills and potentially occludes Tuesday through Friday, expect 
spokes of shortwave energy to pivot it along it. These spokes of 
energy will drive any shower threat, especially in locations along 
and east of I-95. The highest probabilities for rain (at least 
20 percent) remain across southern MD, the northern neck of VA, 
and perhaps northeast MD during the Monday through Friday 
timeframe. Areas further west will likely remain dry with a few 
passing clouds. Downsloping west of the Blue Ridge will keep dry
conditions in place throughout the week. Outside the shower 
chances will be the concern for wind, marine issues, and coastal
flooding. Right now, winds look to average between 15 to 25 mph
during the Monday afternoon through Wednesday afternoon 
timeframe. Highest gusts of 25 to perhaps 35 mph will be down 
across southern MD and along the western shore of the Bay where 
the gradient will be tighter compared to locations west. As for 
marine and coastal flooding concerns see the corresponding 
discussions below. 

Highs temperatures will top out in the mid to upper 60s (50s 
mountains) each day with overnight lows in the upper 30s and mid 
40s. Overnight lows warm into the 50s late week. 

&&

.AVIATION /18Z SATURDAY THROUGH THURSDAY/...
With clouds clearing to the east, the main concern for the TAFs

sunset, although some 15-20 kt gusts may linger the first half

Monday, but a nor'easter will lurk off the Carolina coast. Any 
north or northeasterly gusts to 20 kt will be limited to the 
daytime hours. Dry conditions will continue with few or no 
clouds.

Tuesday through Saturday...Primarily VFR conditions are expected 
amongst the terminals with periods of sub-VFR mainly east of BWI, 
DCA, and MTN. A few showers are possible on the east side of the ZDC

especially near the waters.

Gusty northerly winds continue this afternoon in the wake of a 
strong cold front. Marginal gale gusts continue south of the Bay
Bridge. The Gale Warning continues until 6 AM Sunday, but recent
trends suggest winds may drop below criteria before that point,
perhaps as early as this evening. Elsewhere, Small Craft
Advisories continue. The upper Potomac is expected to drop below

likely won't see wholesale decreases in winds until sometime

.SYNOPSIS...17/256 AM.

A weak to moderate Santa Ana event gusty winds and critical fire 
weather conditions to portions of Southwest California today. In 
addition, the very warm temperatures bring a high risk of heat- 
related illness to all coastal areas. A significant cool down is 
expected Sunday with a good chance of rain Tuesday or Wednesday.

&&

.SHORT TERM (TDY-TUE)...17/151 PM.

For the short term period, 12Z models are in good synoptic
agreement through the period. At upper levels, weak trough will
develop over the area tonight/Sunday then a low will work its way
south, off the CA coast, ending up about 400 miles west of Point
Conception on Tuesday. At the surface, offshore flow will continue
to weaken tonight/Sunday with onshore flow increasing through
Monday and Tuesday.

Forecast-wise, no major changes to previous thinking. With the
pressure gradients relaxing and upper support waning, the Santa
Ana winds will continue to weaken through Sunday morning. So, have
let all WIND ADVISORIES expire at 200 PM this afternoon with
sub-advisory northeast winds expected tonight/Sunday morning. By 
Sunday afternoon, the winds will begin to shift to an onshore 
direction with the onshore flow increasing Monday and Tuesday. Do 
not anticipate any issues with the increasing onshore winds as 
speeds should remain below advisory levels. 

As for temperatures, the combination of increasing onshore flow
and lowering H5 heights/thicknesses will bring a cooling trend to
all areas through Tuesday. The current HEAT ADVISORIES for the
coastal plain should be good to expire at 800 PM this evening. For
Sunday through Tuesday, no heat issues are expected.

As for clouds, there will be some partly cloudy skies across the
area through tonight as high clouds drift up from the south. For
Sunday and Monday, mostly clear skies can be expected although
some marine layer stratus/fog could return to the Central Coast.
On Tuesday, mid and high level clouds should be on the increase
ahead of the upper low, expected to impact the area on Wednesday
and Thursday. Additionally, there should be more widespread marine
layer stratus/fog Monday night/Tuesday morning across the entire
coastal plain and coastal valleys.

.LONG TERM (WED-SAT)...17/151 PM.

For the extended period, 12Z models are in good synoptic
agreement. Main feature of note is a decent, early-season, upper
low. Models move this system east across the area on Wednesday and
Thursday, bringing the high likelihood of wet and unsettled
weather for the area. Admittedly, models will likely be challenged
with such a system in mid-October, so the forecast details could
change noticeably over the coming days. 

That being said, there is rather high confidence in wetting
rainfall across the area in the Tuesday-Thursday time frame,
especially on Wednesday and Thursday. Given the current track of
the upper low, it should be able to tap into some moisture from
the remnants of Trudy. Based on current WPC guidance and ensemble
solutions, a widespread 0.25 to 1.00 inch event is very likely for
the area. However, ensembles indicate, depending on model, about a
20-40% chance for totals greater than 1.00 inch. Southerly flow,
associated with this low, will have the potential to generate some
decent orographic enhancement which could help totals exceed 1.00
inch per those ensemble members. Additionally, there looks to be
some decent instability with the upper low. 500 MB temperatures 
drop to around -20 degrees Celsius and CAPE/MUCAPE values are 
forecast to be in the 400-800 J/kg range. So, there will be a 
chance of thunderstorms on Wednesday and Thursday. 

In terms of rainfall rates, at this time, rates are expected to 
be under 0.50 inches/hour. However, if any thunderstorms do 
develop, locally higher rainfall rates (0.50-1.00 inch/hour) would
be possible. So, there may be some hydrologic concerns as we 
approach the event (mud/debris flows near burn scars, urban 
flooding, etc.). Stay tuned over the coming days for the latest
details.

By Friday and Saturday, the upper low will have move eastward. In
its wake, weak offshore flow is likely. So, expect dry and locally
breezy conditions along with a warming trend.

&&

Today will likely be the last day of widespread high risk of large

of Los Angeles and Ventura Counties where a Red Flag Warning

(peaking in many areas mid morning to mid afternoon) will combine

Cooler and more humid conditions are likely next week. Gusty

Residents in high fire risk areas should be prepared in case a
fire starts. Review your evacuation plans...what would you bring,
where would you go. Stay extra aware of your surroundings. Make
sure your vehicle is fueled up. For everyone, avoid using

scattered showers around the Colorado River Valley as well as across

mild with seasonable temperatures and relatively light winds.

approaches the region, breezy southerly to southwesterly winds will

Tuesday, spreading across the Mojave Desert on Wednesday. In 
addition to gusty winds, this system will also bring increased 
precipitation chances to the region beginning as early as Tuesday 
and continuing as late as Friday. Uncertainty regarding how quickly 
this trough will move through the area continues to result in 
uncertainty regarding the duration of precipitation chances as the 
GFS ensemble mean solution favors a quicker moving trough than its 
ECMWF counterpart. In addition to discrepancies regarding how 
quickly this system moves through the area, there remain 
discrepancies regarding how much moisture will be present, which 
translates to uncertainty regarding precipitation amounts. Cooler 
temperatures will also accompany this trough, with cooler than 
normal temperatures expected during the second half of the week.

.SHORT TERM...

Issued at 219 PM EDT Sat Oct 17 2026

Latest WPC and model sfc analyses place a frontal boundary around
C FL, with GFS/EURO and ensembles showing fair agreement with a 
FROPA across SoFlo through tonight. The front is expected to reach
the Fl Keys by Sunday morning. 

NBM keeps widespread max POPs for the rest of today and tonight in 
the 70-80% range, with numerous showers and scattered thunderstorms 
possible at any time during that time frame. Latest high-res and 
LPMM guidance continues to focus on the east coast metro areas for 
best chances of isolated +6" of rain, which will be exacerbated by 
the weak steering flow prevailing ahead of the FROPA. Because of 
this, WPC has placed all the SoFlo Atlantic metro areas under a 
slight risk of excesssive rainfall (level 2 of 4 / at least 15%), 
and a 1 in 10 chance of Flash Flooding with the heaviest downpours 
and slow moving storms. Main hazards for today and tonight will be 
frequent lightning, damaging wind gusts, and localized flood/flash 
flooding. 

Another weather issue looming for the next few days will be 
increasing northerly wind speeds across the state, with gusty 
periods starting late tonight. This will result in coastal impacts 
over the east coast, including high surf conditions and high rip 
current risk (see the Marine and Beach discussions below). 

Guidance remains consistent in pushing the front through SoFlo and 
stalling it over the Florida Keys by Sunday morning. A modest drying 
trend will follow, but still keeping enough lingering moisture for 
at least scattered showers and storms to develop Sunday, especially 
south of interstate 75.  

Afternoon max temperatures today should remain in the low-mid 80s 
over the Lake region, and into the upper 80s elsewhere. Overnight 
lows should drop into the mid-upper 60s for the western half of 
SoFlo, and into the low-mid 70s across the East Coast. Cooler 
temperatures are expected Sunday, with highs generally in the lower 
to mid 80s across South Florida. 

&&

.LONG TERM...
(Sunday night through Friday)
Issued at 434 AM EDT Sat Oct 17 2026

The frontal boundary remains projected to pass through the area by 
Sunday night while also degrading in the process. This boundary will 
eventually stall over the Florida Straits while diffusing completely 
early this coming week. With moisture levels dropping closer to 
average to below average in some areas, rain chances will lower 
significantly to below 20% for most of interior and SW Florida as 
drier air arrives in the wake of the front. Strong surface high 
pressure will re-develop as the low off the coast of the Carolinas 
begins to advect offshore and shift more towards the Mid-Atlantic 
on, which will create a stout pressure gradient that could last into 
the mid-week time frame. Breezy winds are expected out of the NE 
with wind gusts in the 20-30 mph range possible through Tuesday 
night and potentially a portion of Wednesday. By Wednesday 
afternoon, the pressure gradient should be weakened enough for much 
less breezy conditions. Even with the breezy and gusty winds early 
this week, they should stay below Wind Advisory levels.

The other important aspect of the long term forecast period relates 
to any rain potential through the end of the week. While drier air 
filters in with the passing of the frontal boundary, strong 
northeasterly winds over the local waters will be present in 
combination with slower wind speeds over land, which can result in 
isolated to scattered frictional convergence showers forming along 
the coast. This process is likely to be the main driver in any rain 
shower or storm development through the end of the week, but is not 
expected to produce impactful rainfall or thunderstorms. Instead, 
most of the activity should be of the meager variety. We will 
continue to monitor trends in case a more impactful develops for 
heavy rainfall. High temperatures will fall to the low to mid 80s 
each day in the wake of the front. Overnight lows will range from 
the mid to upper 60s near the lake region to the low to mid 70s 
elsewhere on Monday night, then fall into the 60s across the entire 
region Tuesday night through the end of the week.

.DISCUSSION...
Issued at 157 PM CDT Sat Oct 17 2026

High pressure this afternoon is sliding into Arkansas, bringing to 
an end our brief foray into cooler October weather. Breezy southwest 
winds have developed, with temperatures this afternoon returning to 
near normal levels after a chilly start to the day, which saw our 
first widespread freeze of the season outside of the Twin Cities 
urban core. MSP got down to 36 this morning, the first time MSP has 
dipped below 40 this fall, tying 1931 for the latest first trip 
below 40 in the fall on record.

For the rest of the week, we get into a "stuck" weather pattern. The 
trough currently over the east coast will develop into a cut-off low 
in the western Atlantic as ridge builds over the top of it from the 
Plains to New England. This ridge will push the northern stream back 
north into Canada, allowing a very mild airmass to overspread the 
CONUS east of the Rockies. We'll have highs in the 60s Monday and 
Tuesday, but from Wednesday into next weekend, highs in the 70s will 
become rather common. Fortunately, these warmer temperatures will 
come with dewpoints in the 50s, which will keep us front having any 
significant fire weather concerns. The next chance rain has now 
pushed off to next weekend, when a weakening cold front is forecast 
to make a run into the ridge. Given the forcing looks week and the 
antecedent airmass is warm and dry, I wouldn't count on these rain 
chances remaining in the forecast as next weekend moves into the 5 
days or less period. 

Finally, through the first half of October, the average temperature 
at MSP was 60 degrees. A full 7 degrees warmer than normal and 0.8 
degrees warmer than 1947, the current warmest October on record. 
We're now getting into the "cold half" of October, which should 
start chipping away at that average temperature, but there's very 
little in the way of cold air highlighted by the ensembles for the 
rest of the month and it may be tough for us to chip away at our 
lead enough to not finish in the top spot for warmest October on 
record. Something to watch over the next couple of weeks.

.SHORT TERM /Today through Sunday/... 
Pronounced Rex blocking currently over the western Conus will 
transition into a more progressive pattern over the next 48 hours as 
strong jet energy entering the East Pacific acts to deamplify the 
ridge axis while also forcing the absorption the associated southern 
stream cutoff low into the mean westerly flow aloft. The latter of 
these two processes will take much longer for completion resulting 
in a prolonged period of southerly moist advection through the H7-H5 
layer yielding total column PWATS in excess of 1" across much of the 
CWA. This pattern configuration will also place south-central Arizona 
within a favorable ascent position in relation to an upper level jet 
streak able to tap some of this thick midlevel moisture. However, 
the sfc-H8 layer remain exceptionally dry due to persistent 
downsloping easterly winds, and this deep sub-cloud dry layer will 
need to be at least partially moistened before more notable chances 
of measurable rain can be achieved. Based on the synoptic ascent 
structure, a weakening easterly low level gradient, and trends in 
regional WV imagery, feel this evolution will be more effective than 
suggested by base NBM POPS, and have boosted the chances for light 
accumulations through Sunday morning. 

Forecast uncertainty Sunday afternoon and evening is greater than 
usual for a 24-48 time frame with some measure of midlevel cyclonic 
flow hovering over south-central Arizona as the upper wave only 
slowly gets stretched and deamplifies. Moisture should gradually 
become scoured from the cloud layer as winds veer more 
southwesterly, but the process may be more delayed with the slow 
transition. Thus, its not out of the question a few light showers 
linger throughout the day, though becoming primarily focused in 
orographically favored areas east of Phoenix. By Sunday evening, the 
upper low will finally begin ejecting into northern Arizona, but 
even so, moist upslope through Gila County could still support a 
couple isolated light showers into Monday morning. 

&&

.LONG TERM /Monday through Friday/...
By early next week, high pressure will be well established over NE 
CONUS, while the aforementioned wave becomes absorbed into the mean 
SW flow head of the next incoming low pressure system diving down 
the west coast. Another low chance (20-30%) of showers may be 
manifested Monday morning across the higher terrain of south-central 
Arizona , however if anything does develop, total accumulations are 
expected to be minimal. By Tuesday, deep troughing and strong 
negative height anomalies will amplify and intensify along the west 
coast, however confidence in the timing and depth of this feature 
remains low to moderate. The deterministic ECMWF forecasts a slower 
and deeper solution yielding a more robust rainfall scenario, while 
the GFS deterministic provides a faster outcome lifting the cold 
core into southern Utah resulting in a more tempered rainfall 
potential. Regardless, the timing of the best rainfall potential is 
highlighting the Wednesday and Thursday time frame while pattern 
recognition and some instability parameters suggest the potential for 
strong thunderstorms ahead of the shortwave passage. Additionally, 
with the uncertainty of this next system, a wide spread in NBM 
temperatures have presented themselves throughout the week, though 
below normal highs are most likely.

.PREV DISCUSSION...

DISCUSSION...

Pretty quiet forecast heading through the end of the work week as 
the energetic jet stream resides mostly across Canada. Stacked low 
centered over Hudson Bay today will send a trough down through the 
Great Lakes on the nose of a mid level jet streak tonight. This 
opens the door for broad troughing to encompass a portion of the 
northern Great Lakes while high pressure slides through the Midwest 
into the Ohio Valley building a stable airmass across the southern 
Great Lakes. For tonight, northwesterly cool flow over the 
relatively warm lakes will provide a boost to instability and though 
moisture is weak, PWATs roughly 0.6 inches, there could be enough 
concentrated moisture in the region of steeper low/mid level lapse 
rates to allow some scattered showers or even a thunderstorm over 
the north half of Lake Huron. Further south into the Thumb, moisture 
is even thinner and forcing weaker, but the cool airmass and low 
level jet could be enough to touch off some scattered showers over 
the Thumb this evening into tonight. Current radar over the U.P. 
does have thunderstorms present adding to the confidence of weak 
storms over northern Huron later. 

High pressure then expands back northward across the region ending 
any rain chances Thursday into Friday. Cool air within the trough 
will drop 850mb temps into the single digits above 0C leading to 
cool highs in the 60s to end the week. Clearing skies under the 
ridge with the cool airmass in place could allow some low temps to 
fall into the upper 30s Thursday night in some of the cooler spots, 
otherwise low 40s could be in store for most locations. 

Brief but strong warm up on Saturday as strong ridging over the 
Plains advances eastward over the Great Lakes. ECMWF is a touch 
warmer (~18C at 850mb) than GFS (-16C) Saturday with strong 
southwesterly flow into the region. Current forecast is for temps to 
touch 80F in the Saginaw Valley with upper 70s for most other 
locations. The warm front leading the way could touch off a few 
showers after 00Z Saturday with the bubble of stronger theta e 
lifting through the area. Though model output is not strong in 
producing rain, we've see these leading theta e gradients on 
elevated warm fronts produce narrow brief areas of showers many 
times. For now, we'll note it and see if we need to add POPs later. 

This warmup will be brief as attention the turns to TS Isaias which 
is set to make landfall over MS Friday evening then getting drawn 
northward into the Ohio Valley before getting caught in the 
westerlies and forced to the east coast. This brings the rain shield 
into Lower MI Saturday night and/or Sunday. Details will come 
together in the coming days, but for now expect a gradient of rain 
from south to north with the highest totals over southern lower MI. 
Abundant moisture with a tropical system will lead to efficient rain 
production for any areas that get clipped by the rain shield.

MARINE...

Moderate southwesterly winds gradually weaken this evening as a cold 
front extending from low pressure near James Bay crosses the central 
Great Lakes. The lighter gradient winds also veer west-northwesterly 
behind the front early tonight. However, an uptick in speeds returns 
late tonight or early Wednesday as the upper level jet deepens over 
the region. Stability trends lower with the slightly cooler airmass, 
and given the rejuvenated low-level jet winds, mixing likely 
delivers some elevated gusts. Potential exists for gusts to around 
30 knots over portions of Lake Huron Thursday afternoon, with 
marginal gusts to gales possible for northern Huron. A Small Craft 
Advisory may be needed over The Thumb should confidence rise in the 
frequency of 25+ knot gusts, but any higher end gusts further north 
should be infrequent enough to preclude a Gale Warning. Mid/Upper 
Mississippi Valley high pressure then expands into the area Thursday 
night and Friday offering weaker winds with a southerly shift.

.DISCUSSION (This evening through Saturday)...
Issued at 124 PM EDT Sat Oct 17 2026

Tonight Through Sunday Night.

Surface high pressure centered across the Mid-Mississippi Valley 
this afternoon will drift east across Indiana tonight, establishing 
optimal conditions for boundary layer decoupling. Strong synoptic 
subsidence in the wake of the exiting upper trough will maintain 
clear skies. Light and variable to calm winds are anticipated across 
the entire forecast area after 02Z with temperatures rapidly 
dropping out of the mid 50s and into the low 40s by late this 
evening. 

The primary forecast challenge continues to center on overnight 
minimum temperatures and associated frost/freeze headlines. The 
aforementioned efficient radiational cooling will allow for 
temperatures to drop into the low to mid 30s across all of central 
Indiana with uncertainty remaining as to where the best chances for 
sub-freezing temperatures will be. As of early this afternoon, dew 
points remain generally at or above 32 but expect at least some 
additional drops as northerly to northeasterly flow continues. NBM 
continues to run on the cooler side of most hi-res guidance with the 
Canadian and its associated ensemble pushing down the mean, but with 
such efficient radiational cooling expected the Canadian may be 
closer to reality than the HRRR/NAM. The WRF-ARW which similarly 
handles efficient radiational cooling shows temperatures near to 
below freezing for much of central Indiana. Thus, generally expect 
all areas to see a widespread frost with more rural areas to see 
temperatures at or below freezing. Urban areas will end up a degree 
or two above, but with the uncertainty as to where the freeze will 
occur, not planning on adjusting the headlines at this time.

By Sunday, the surface anticyclone center slips eastward into the 
upper Ohio Valley and central Appalachians. Low-level flow will back 
to the south-southwest at 5 to 10 mph by afternoon. Model soundings 
show a dry atmospheric column with precipitable water values under 
0.35 inches, supporting abundant sunshine. Boundary layer mixing up 
to approximately 900mb where temperatures recover to 6C to 8C will 
allow afternoon maximum temperatures to rebound into the lower to 
mid 60s. For Sunday night, modest south-southwesterly return flow 
will keep the boundary layer slightly mixed, holding minimum 
temperatures in the upper 30s to lower 40s and precluding 
significant frost concerns outside of isolated sheltered depressions.

Monday Through Saturday.

The medium-range period will be characterized by a stagnant, highly 
amplified synoptic regime featuring ridging over the eastern third 
of the CONUS and a deep closed trough digging into the Western 
States. With surface high pressure anchored off the Mid-Atlantic 
coast, persistent low-level southwesterly flow will advect a much 
milder continental airmass northward. 850mb temperatures are 
forecast to warm from 9C on Monday to near 13C to 15C by Wednesday 
and Thursday. Under mostly sunny to partly cloudy skies, daytime 
highs will peak in the upper 60s to lower 70s on Monday, reaching 
the mid to upper 70s Tuesday through Thursday, which is roughly 10 
to 15 degrees above seasonal normals. Overnight lows will 
concurrently moderate into the 40s Monday night and the lower to mid 
50s for the remainder of the week.

Dry weather will dominate the regional sensible weather through at 
least Thursday night due to deep-layer subsidence, strong capping 
around 800mb, and the diversion of synoptic moisture plumes well 
northwest into the Upper Midwest. Toward the Friday and Saturday 
timeframe, deterministic solutions diverge regarding the ejection 
speed of the western trough into the northern Plains. There are some 
signs that there may be a decaying frontal boundary nearing the area 
by late Friday but confidence is low in any precipitation chances 
with the strong ridging in place ahead of time.

.SHORT TERM /THROUGH SUNDAY NIGHT/...
Issued at 139 PM CDT Sat Oct 17 2026

The short term will be dominated by a cooler Canadian air mass 
with high pressure centered over the forecast area today. The 
main forecast challenge is the extent of frost tonight into 
early Sunday morning, and to a degree additional frost 
potential Sunday night.

The center of the surface high will shift eastward into the Ohio 
Valley tonight at the same time an upper ridge builds across the 
southern Plains. The continuation of clear skies will be one 
frost factor though attention to surface winds will be the 
dominant frost factor. Expectations are that the surface high 
will shift eastward enough for winds generally north of the 
Plateau and west of Highway 5 to maintain enough mixing after 
midnight. Consequently will lean toward the lower end of the 
model spectrum in the sheltered areas south and east of this 
region and in particular the eastern Ozarks resulting in these 
areas standing the best chance for frost. 

Sunday will then begin a warming trend as the upper ridge builds 
east while cyclogenesis occurs over the Rockies leading to a 
strengthening low level southerly flow that will continue into
coming work week.

&&

.LONG TERM /MONDAY THROUGH FRIDAY/...
Issued at 139 PM CDT Sat Oct 17 2026

To what should be no surprise given trends this summer, our weekend 
spell of cooler fall weather will be short lived as the region will 
once again see temperatures shoot up over the coming week as upper 
heights climb above 585 with the return of the southern upper ridge. 
The NBM models depict a 25-75 percentile spread of only a few 
degrees apart leading to high confidence in this warming trend.

Of equal note is that the dry Canadian continental air mass has
advected all the way into the Gulf so even with the return flow
this week the pattern will keep the vertical pattern dry 
leading to a extremely low chance for any rainfall minimizing 
any recent improvements to the drought gained by last weeks 
rainfall. 

As had been previously introduced, there remains at least medium
confidence in above normal temperatures to end October as the 
CPC has our entire region in a 60-70% chance for above normal 
temperatures for the period of October 24-30.

&&

.SHORT TERM /THROUGH SUNDAY NIGHT/...
Issued at 144 PM CDT Sat Oct 17 2026

As of early this afternoon, a broad surface ridge axis stretches 
from Lake Michigan southwestward through the region, which has aided 
in the continuation of calm/variable winds and a clear sky today. 
This surface ridge axis will slide southeastward into the evening, 
becoming centered over the southeastern half of the area tonight. As 
a result, the coolest temperatures by tomorrow morning (mid 30s) are 
forecast along and to the south of I-44 in MO and I-70 in IL, where 
a Frost Advisory remains in effect until 9am Sunday. Some river 
valley/low-lying locations across the area mentioned above will be 
the coldest with some localized areas that may approach the freezing 
mark. The remainder of the area should cool off into the upper 30s 
to lower 40s tonight. These seasonably cool temperatures combined 
with the warm water temperatures that remain in area lakes/rivers 
may result in areas of steam fog that could be locally dense early 
in the morning before fading shortly after sunrise.

A quicker warmup will be in store on Sunday compared to what was 
realized today, as 850mb temperatures will be about 10C warmer by 
Sunday morning than this morning. The warmer low-level temperatures, 
coupled with light southerly flow and abundant sunshine, should 
result in highs that reach the mid 60s to lower 70s by tomorrow 
afternoon. The surface ridge axis should remain near the 
southeastern half of the area Sunday night, which may allow for 
another night of efficient radiational cooling, resulting in lows 
that could reach the mid 30s for some leading to patchy frost.

&&

.LONG TERM /MONDAY THROUGH SATURDAY/...
Issued at 144 PM CDT Sat Oct 17 2026

For nearly the entire week, the prevailing large-scale pattern will 
feature mid-level troughing across the Pacific Coast with ridging 
centered from the Central Plains to the Middle Mississippi Valley. A 
gradual warmup is forecast through the week as LREF 850mb 
temperatures slowly climb from near 10C at the beginning of the week 
into the low teens (10-14C) by mid-late week. The NBM continues to 
be on the warmer end of guidance but has come down a few degrees on 
the latest run. Now it is more closely aligned with other members 
and more representable of the low-level airmass (850mb temperatures) 
that the LREF indicates. As a result, the latest LREF temperature 
IQRs reveal near normal temperatures are expected into Tuesday with 
above normal temperatures forecast to make a comeback by Thursday 
lasting into next Saturday. Mid-level ridging remains nearly 
stationary across the area this week, resulting in high confidence 
that dry conditions prevail into next Saturday.

&&

.AVIATION /18Z TAFS THROUGH 00Z MONDAY/...
Issued at 1237 PM CDT Sat Oct 17 2026

Light and variable surface winds continue this afternoon into 
tonight as a surface ridge axis slides sewd across the region. With 
these light winds and lows forecast in the mid 30s, steam fog along 
area rivers should develop tonight. While confidence is relatively 
high in areas of river steam fog tonight, especially along the 
Missouri and Mississippi Rivers, confidence is low if this fog ends 
up impacting the nearby terminals. Any steam fog that develops has 
the best chance to impact visibilities is at KSUS, KJEF, and 
possibly KCPS, most likely between 09-14z Sunday morning. With lower 
confidence regarding this potential, opted to leave mention out of 
the TAFs for now. Dry and VFR conditions are expected for the 
remaining terminals through Sunday.
